News
LA’s city attorney used tax dollars to pay her court penalty. A complaint claims that’s illegal
Nick Gerda
is an accountability reporter who has covered local government in Southern California for more than a decade.
Published November 27, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
L.A. City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto at a news conference.
Carlin Stiehl
Los Angeles Times via Getty Images )
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto and her chief deputy used city taxpayer money to pay court penalties that a judge imposed on each of them this month, according to records their office released to LAist on Tuesday.
On Nov. 4, Feldstein Soto and Denise Mills each signed a request for a $1,000 check from the office's petty cash fund to pay the sanctions, which were paid to the court last week through city checks, the records show.
Then, the day after LAist filed the records request seeking all records about the payments, Feldstein Soto wrote the city a $1,000 personal check to reimburse the sanctions payment, the records show. The records released to LAist do not show repayment from Mills.
Feldstein Soto and Mills have not responded to multiple requests for comment, including about whether this was an illegal use of tax dollars. Their office spokesperson responded only by saying last week that the records would be released.
L.A. County Superior Court Judge Brock T. Hammond ordered the sanctions on Nov. 2, after finding that Feldstein Soto had “evaded compliance” with a subpoena and a court order to turn over messages about Michelle McGinnis, a former top prosecutor in the office who says Feldstein Soto fired her for speaking up about alleged wrongdoing. He also found that both women's sworn statements and logs of withheld records had not complied with a May court order.
Both Feldstein Soto and Mills told the court they had complied with the order. Feldstein Soto said in a sworn statement that she “did not withhold or delete any text messages; I simply did not have any on any of my devices or in any of my accounts.” Feldstein Soto and the city's lawyers also deny McGinnis' retaliation claims.
The judge imposed the sanctions on Feldstein Soto and Mills, not on the city, according to the court’s official record. Attorneys for the city, whose litigation is managed by Feldstein Soto’s office, emphasized in a court filing last week that the case was filed against both women "in their individual capacities," and that the city "is not a party to these proceedings."
Sponsored message
City attorney procedures, with an effective date under Feldstein Soto’s administration, say petty cash can be used to pay sanctions but don’t explain the authority for it, nor whether it applies only to cases in which the city is a party. The citywide rules for petty cash do not list sanctions as an allowed use, and state law bars officials from using public resources for “personal or other purposes which are not authorized by law.” The city attorney’s petty cash policy was disclosed in the records request.
Backstory on the penalties
The sanctions came in a lawsuit McGinnis filed in court to enforce her subpoenas for records, as she appeals her firing through the city’s arbitration process.
McGinnis ran the office's criminal branch until she was placed on leave in April 2024 and fired in January 2025. She alleges her ouster was payback for objecting to conduct by Feldstein Soto that she believed was illegal. McGinnis has an earlier lawsuit against the city for whistleblower retaliation. That’s a separate case from the one where sanctions were ordered, which was against Feldstein Soto and Mills individually.
Feldstein Soto and the city's lawyers say McGinnis was disciplined for doing outside work without approval and failing to fix problems with the office's access to criminal history databases. In their court filing last week, the city's lawyers also alleged “a pattern of insubordination.”
A judge last year allowed McGinnis' whistleblower retaliation lawsuit to move forward, finding that the city's evidence “falls far short of conclusively establishing” that she was disciplined for legitimate reasons.
McGinnis subpoenaed Feldstein Soto and Mills for their messages about her, including texts between the two of them. Hammond, the judge, later issued a court order directing both women to comply with the subpoena.
Sponsored message
Hammond ruled this month that it is “undisputed” that Feldstein Soto has not turned over a single responsive text message, and he ordered a forensic search of her devices. He ordered each woman to pay $1,000 “for non-compliance with the Court's order,” writing that both gave “insufficient or nonexistent explanations” for missing records. On Monday, the judge denied the city's request to throw out the ruling.
What the payment records show
Mills set the payments in motion. In a Nov. 4 email, she asked her assistant to prepare petty cash requests “for Hydee in the amount of $1,000 and for me in the amount of $1,000.”
The forms both women signed requesting the city funds have a section for the “justification,” which asks requesters to check one of 18 categories. “Do not leave blank,” it states.
The records show the justification section was left blank on the request forms, which were signed by Feldstein Soto and Mills.
The payment requests include a memo from Mills, which did not cite the legal authority for having the city pay the sanctions.

Bruins and Trojans face off in the ‘Battle for LA’ — the whole city will be watching
Jolie Lash
is wearing blue and gold to the game, much to her father's chagrin
Published November 27, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
Tommy Trojan on the USC campus, the Bruin bear on the UCLA campus
Genaro Molina/Christina House
Getty Images)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
“You gotta choose a side at some point, right? The world asks you in L.A. to pick your side.” That’s just a bit of how UCLA football head coach Bob Chesney, in his first season in Westwood, responded to reporters this week when asked about the crosstown matchup with the USC Trojans (8-3) at the Rose Bowl Saturday.
The annual game, dubbed the “Battle for L.A.,” is part of a crosstown rivalry dating back to 1929. In nearly a century, it’s become part of our local lore and traditions, intertwined with our personal histories as Southern Californians.
For me, it’s a well-decorated section of the tapestry of my childhood memories, and now my adulthood as well; and for many of us locals, something a bit more complicated than picking a side.
USC mascot statue Tommy Trojan is covered against vandalism on the USC campus ahead of rivalry weekend football game against UCLA on Thursday, Nov. 16, 2023, in Los Angeles, California.
Brian van der Brug
Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Growing up a Trojan
As a kid, my side was chosen for me as I rode up in the backseat of a cardinal-colored sedan; my Trojan alum dad taking us up the 5, onto the 110, to the SC campus for home games. During those grade- and middle school years, SC traditions — strolling past the sealed-up Tommy Trojan statue (to prevent the Bruins from dumping blue paint over it. UCLA students do the same for “The Bruin” bear on their campus), meeting up at alumni tents to tailgate and kicking a specific light-post base for good luck as we followed the Trojan Marching Band pied piper style to the L.A. Memorial Coliseum for the biggest (and certainly the loudest) game of the season — became mine. For a time.
UCLA's Bruin Bear in protective covering to protect it from vandalism at UCLA on Wednesday, Nov. 15, 2023, in Los Angeles, California
Irfan Khan
Los Angeles Times)
Sponsored message
How I became a Bruin
Fast forward to adulthood, and eventually, through work, I ended up a Bruin. It’s basically sacrilegious to do or admit that, and something my dad likes to rib me about, but I’ve been proudly cheering on the blue and gold, even when there wasn’t much football fun to shout about (though the Jerry Neuheisel-called offensive plays last season in the victory over top 10-ranked Penn State were pure delight).
The Bruin fans I've met this season
Going to the games at the Rose Bowl this fall, I’ve crossed paths with a host of Bruin supporters whose own journeys to pick a side took many routes. During the home opener against San Diego State, I encountered a group of friends, none of whom went to UCLA. They picked the Bruins as their team when they were in high school, and their love for the sons of Westwood became an adult tradition that sees them meeting up throughout the fall for home games.
At this year’s homecoming game, amid a sea of blue on the packed home side of the stadium, a gentleman behind me whose legs were so long they couldn’t help but brush the edge of my seat turned out to be a former player under legendary UCLA coach Terry Donahue, for whom the Rose Bowl Pavilion is named.
Sponsored message
The Rose Bowl Stadium on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026
Jolie Lash
LAist)
Another game day, I shared armrests with the aunt of one of UCLA’s players, who shouted for her nephew whenever he took the field. Our section joined her in loudly cheering him on. Then, two weeks ago, in the drenching rain of Friday, the 13th, seated among late ’60s alums and high school-aged fans, we all jumped out of our seats and applauded quarterback Ty Dieffenbach as he jogged his way back onto the field after an injury took him out of the Illinois matchup right before halftime. (After an injury in overtime at Michigan last week, Dieffenbach’s status for Saturday’s game is unclear.)
The Battle of L.A.
UCLA vs. USC at Rose Bowl in Pasadena
Kick off: Saturday, Nov. 27, at 12:30 p.m.
Watch on TV: CBS, or stream it via Paramount+ with a Paramount+ Premium subscription
As of press time, some tickets were still available through the UCLA Athletics website.
Why anything can happen Saturday
It’s been a joyful season cheering on UCLA, but going into Saturday’s game, where I will likely be a lone blue shirt among a solid section of cardinal (I chose visitor-side tickets because I was going to take my dad, but he hurt his foot!), one truth from my childhood stands out: At the UCLA-USC crosstown rivalry game, anything can happen.
It doesn’t matter which team is higher in the AP college football rankings before kickoff (UCLA this year), or if the other team boasts a Heisman Trophy winner on his way to being picked No. 1 in the NFL draft (USC in 2023 with Caleb Williams — they lost). This year, the smart money says it’s truly a toss-up.
Sponsored message
Whether 1946, 1996 or 2026, the players feel peak emotions and there’s always tension on the field. In the stands, even in a venue like the Rose Bowl, which sits in the sound-dissipating hollow of the Arroyo Seco, fans, on their chosen side, will be fired up like no other game of the fall. This is the one that decides whose colors coat the Victory Bell for a year, and more importantly, who gets bragging rights in L.A.

Tang’s Donut in Silver Lake closed 13 years ago. Its sign just found a new home
Fiona Ng
is LAist's deputy managing editor and leads a team of reporters who explore food, culture, history, events and more.
Published November 28, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
Tang's Donut sign has found a new home in Y-Que Trading Post in Los Feliz.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
A donut shop has sat hollowed out and vacant at Sunset Boulevard and Fountain Avenue in Silver Lake — a neighborhood relic frozen in place for more than a decade. All that remains are the red-on-yellow Tang’s Donut & Sandwiches signs from its past lives — a mom-and-pop donut joint, a refuge for all-night chess and the starting point of a renegade street bike club.
Now, after murmurs that a new tenant may finally be moving in, one of the signs has found a new home.
“Yeah, I'd kinda been stalking it for a long time,” said Bill Wyatt, proud new owner of the Tang’s Donut sign.
Tang's Donut closed in 2013. Its signs never came down.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
The Tangs gave Bill Wyatt their blessing to keep one of the storefront signs.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
How a donut shop became an unusual Silver Lake hangout
Jenny Tang and her family operated their eponymous donut shop starting in the mid-1980s, according to the L.A. Times, in a strip mall up the street from my middle school. I remember walking past the joint, indistinguishable from other donut joints in the city. An Orange Bang machine. A couple of arcade games. Display cases filled with deep-fried, sugary goodness.
Somewhere along the way, Tang’s outdoor patio became the unlikely spot for a motley crew to gather to play chess, often well into the night. I had seen the crowd from across the street in the 2000s, while catching a smoke outside of Akbar.
Sponsored message
The all-night chess scene at Tang's in 2006.
Terry Chen
Courtesy Terry Chen)
Lisa Willis found belonging in that thriving chess scene while she was experiencing homelessness.
“On Saturdays really strong blitz players would show up, I heard one was an International Chess Federation master, but who knows?” she wrote in a 2022 essay in Street Sheet, published by the Coalition on Homelessness in San Francisco. “On a typical night it was just us mere mortals playing.”
Bill Wyatt started making and selling Tang's Donut T-shirts about a decade ago.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
Willis wrote about the people she played with: a man around 80 nicknamed Kamikaze who was in the Chinese army; Key, about 70, from Vietnam; Walter, whom she played blitz against until sunrise.
The immigrant family running the shop, she wrote, was kind to everyone. “I was homeless for nine straight months, and that place was like my home,” Willis wrote. She did not respond to my requests for comment.
“There were always people hanging out there,” Wyatt said. He also owns Y-Que Trading Post, a T-shirt store in Los Feliz. “Some were playing chess, but some were just hanging out all day or sitting there.”
Sponsored message
When Wyatt got the Tangs’ blessing to take the donut sign, he asked Mr. Tang about the chess players. Tang told him he had never considered anyone “an inconvenience or a burden.”
‘Tang’s at 10’: The start of a bike movement
View this post on Instagram
In 2005, the donut shop became the starting point for Wolfpack Hustle, a weekly night ride for street cyclists rolling out at 10 p.m. on Mondays — before Ward launched an L.A. Marathon version.
“We started out just meeting at Tang's spontaneously,” said Don Ward, the founder of Wolfpack Hustle.
Ward and his friends called these weekly rides Tang’s at 10, before they blew up into an event that drew hundreds.  One of those riders was a Tang’s chess regular, Ward said. And their team jerseys all bore Tang’s logo.
“How do I get a dang sign!” Ward said when I reached out to him to chat. “I’ve always wanted to harvest one.”
Sponsored message
View this post on Instagram
Still vacant after more than a decade
Tang's Donut on December 27, 2013. Emily Morrill, who worked next door at Garage Pizza and took the photo, said the shop closed that night.
Emily Morrill
Courtesy Emily Morrill)
After 13 years, Tang’s still sits empty. Memories and hijinks never stopped. In 2014, a photo posted on social media showed a “Wu” tagged in front of the sign so it read “Wu Tang’s Donuts.”
About a year ago, Wyatt said he started noticing construction at the location. He started to drop by every couple of weeks and left his name and contact information with the workers.
He got a call a few months ago, saying that the Tangs themselves were at the old storefront. That’s when Wyatt made the ask.
“I learned a lot about the history of the Cambodian donut empires that existed in L.A. [and that] they were part of,” Wyatt said.
Sponsored message
View this post on Instagram
How the sign ended up in Los Feliz
As for the Silver Lake Tang’s, word on the street is that a Thai place is moving in. Wyatt said he talked to the new tenants, who also gave him the all-clear to take the sign.
Two weeks ago, Wyatt installed it inside Y-Que Trading Post. He was worried the patina was dulling from the many, many Tang’s fans coming in to touch the ampersand for good luck.
Now, Tang’s Donut & Sandwiches is right where it should be, on the wall across from another Silver Lake icon Wyatt nabbed — the happy/sad foot sign for a podiatrist that once had an office inside another Sunset Boulevard strip mall.
Bill Wyatt standing in front of the famed Silver Lake "happy foot/sad foot" sign.
Fiona Ng
LAist)

Westlake tenants push back against landlord’s plan to replace parking lot with ADUs
By Isaac Ceja | The LA Local
Published November 27, 2026 at 11:00 AM PST
Tenants Aminda Cabrera, left, and Alejandra Bueno, right, pose for a portrait at the parking at their apartment building in Westlake in Los Angeles on Nov. 6, 2026.
Isaac Ceja
The LA Local)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
This story first appeared on The LA Local.
Ana Rodriguez has lived in the same Westlake apartment for 43 years.
She still has the same dining table where she helped her daughter, now a mother herself, complete her math homework and Rodriguez remembers sleeping in her car along with her neighbors for over a week after the 1994 Northridge earthquake.
While she thought she’d be able to retire comfortably paying just over $750 a month in rent, Rodriguez, now 68, is concerned about her living situation. A new landlord bought the property earlier this year and plans to convert the apartment complex’s parking lot into accessory dwelling units (ADUs).
“They want to give us a minimal amount [of money] to pay for us to give them the parking spots, but in reality there’s no space outside where we’d be able to park,” Rodriguez said.
Ana Rodriguez, center left, and Alejandra Bueno, center right, attend a tenants union meeting in Los Angeles on Nov. 5, 2026.
Isaac Ceja
The LA Local)
Parking in the neighborhood is difficult where many residents park their vehicles on red curbs, street corners or otherwise pay around $200 at private lots. The tenants also claim that there have been car break-ins in the neighborhood.
Sponsored message
Nisan Emunah Ventures LLC purchased the property in mid-2026 and began removing services like on-site laundry and gardening maintenance, and wants to convert the parking lot into bachelor apartments or ADUs.
Rodriguez and her neighbors, who have all lived in the building for at least 20 years, formed the Valley Tenants Association in September, which includes 6 out of the 7 currently occupied units at the apartment complex on West Valley Street.
According to the tenants, they are fighting for parking spaces and amenities that are included in their housing contract.
Records from the Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety show the owner has approved permits to construct eight ADUs on the parking lot.
Since 2025, the state of California has allowed for up to eight detached ADUs on existing multifamily properties. Senate Bill 1211 restricts local agencies from requiring replacement parking when existing spaces are converted into ADUs.
According to Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety records, the number of permits issued for ADUs on existing multifamily dwellings per the new state law increased from 78 in 2025 to 198 so far in 2026 in the city of Los Angeles.
The top neighborhood for these permits is Westlake with 15 approvals in 2026, according to the latest available data and compiled by Crosstown.
Sponsored message
A view of the apartment building at 2334 Valley Street in Westlake in Los Angeles on Nov. 6, 2026.
Isaac Ceja
The LA Local)
For almost a year now, tenants across Los Angeles have been fighting against the construction of ADUs in parking spaces, which some view as violence against tenants, while housing advocacy groups view the situation as a win for new housing construction in the state.
Housing advocates like California YIMBY have championed the legislation to address the state’s housing crisis.
The tenants at the Valley Street apartments have received notices about the ADU project for months now. The LA Local contacted a listed representative, Eliza Kerndian, about the tenants’ demands regarding the loss of their parking. A representative with Nisan Emunah Ventures LLC responded to questions via a written statement.
The statement said they recognize “the importance of housing stability, quality of life and the daily needs of existing residents” and respect residents’ right to express those concerns.
The statement added that the owner’s priority is to find a mutually acceptable solution consistent with local laws and respectful of the rights of all parties. They welcomed any help from the Los Angeles Housing Department, the City Attorney’s Dispute Resolution Program, or any independent mediation organization.
“Ownership is prepared to participate in good-faith mediation to better understand residents’ needs, evaluate practical alternatives and explore potential solutions within the applicable regulatory framework,” the statement said.
Sponsored message
Councilmember Hugo Soto-Martinez’s (CD-13) office has met with affected residents and said his office is pushing for a resolution that addresses their concerns and protects their rights.
Nick Barnes-Batista, communications director for CD-13, said the councilmember’s office has formally requested written confirmation that all construction activities at the property cease until management has adequately addressed the tenants’ outstanding concerns.
In a written statement, the councilmember’s office asked that management not tow tenants’ vehicles, ensure they have access to their existing parking spaces and other requests from tenants.
‘It’s not an indulgence’
The Valley Street tenants have been met with constant announcements of demolition and construction beginning on the parking lot and have been hosting sit-ins with people constantly rotating throughout the day.
Alejandra Bueno, who has lived in the apartment complex for 30 years, began protesting by sitting in the parking lot along w
